headline: A tornado killed hundreds in March, Tennessee tried a teacher in July, and Baird sent a face down a wire
texture: The Tri-State Tornado crossed Missouri, Illinois and Indiana on March 18 and remains the deadliest in American history. In July a Dayton court tried John Scopes for teaching evolution, in a case staged for the purpose, and the argument was carried out in front of a national press. Nellie Tayloe Ross took office in Wyoming on January 5 as the first woman to govern a state.

John Logie Baird transmitted the first television picture in London on October 2, a recognisable human face in a laboratory. The Locarno Treaties were negotiated in October and signed in London on December 1, an attempt to fix the borders the last war had left. Hitler published the first volume of Mein Kampf on July 18, out of prison and setting out what he meant to do.

The Big Parade took $4,990,000 in rentals, with Ben-Hur just behind it and Chaplin's The Gold Rush fourth. Fitzgerald published The Great Gatsby in New York on April 10 to modest sales. The Phantom of the Opera brought Lon Chaney's face to a screen that was still silent, and audiences reportedly fainted. Friedrich Ebert, the first president of Germany, died in February and was replaced by a field marshal.

Two claims here are general knowledge of the subject rather than statements from the year pages, and come out if they cannot be confirmed: that Gatsby sold modestly at first, and that audiences fainted at Chaney's unmasking. Ebert's successor is described as a field marshal without naming him, because the source line does not.
